extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning discrete mathematics, combinatorics, and proof techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Introductory textbook guidance on combinatorial counting (binomial coefficients, Pascal's triangle, inclusion–exclusion, addition principle) and on writing/verifying direct proofs (definitions, proofs, strategies, notation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof must be understandable and convincing
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof of a theorem is a written verification that shows the theorem is definitely and unequivocally true; it should be understandable and convincing to anyone who has the requisite background and knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure readers share the agreed meanings of the mathematical words, phrases and symbols used. Use clear logical steps and standard facts; avoid ambiguity. A proof should be structured so a knowledgeable reader can follow and be convinced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions must be exact and unambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition is an exact, unambiguous explanation of the meaning of a mathematical word or phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase definitions clearly (technically 'if and only if' but commonly written as 'if' for brevity). Use definitions when proving statements (e.g., 'n is odd' ⇒ n = 2a + 1 for some integer a). Mark defined terms clearly (book uses boldface).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use definitions to transform assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving, apply the definitions relevant to your hypothesis to rewrite assumptions in concrete algebraic or structural form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: use Definition of odd/even to write x = 2a or x = 2a+1; use Definition of divisibility a|b to write b = a·c. These substitutions are standard first steps in direct proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguous or overloaded notation; rename reused symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful not to reuse variable names/letters in conflicting contexts; avoid confusing expressions by distinguishing statements and numeric expressions (e.g., a|b vs a/b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a symbol already appears with a different meaning, pick a fresh letter (the text replaces c by d or e in examples). Explicitly point out when an expression is a statement (a|b) versus a number (a/b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct proof outline (assume P then show Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'If P, then Q' by direct proof, begin by assuming P is true and show this forces Q to be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical structure: 'Proof. Suppose P. [logical steps using definitions and facts] Therefore Q. ■' Focus only on the P-true cases because when P is false the implication is vacuously true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'Proof.' and an end-of-proof marker
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate clearly the beginning and end of a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with the word 'Proof.' and end with a symbol (the text uses '■') or an explicit 'Therefore ...' to show completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write first and last lines first, then fill in (top-bottom/back-and-forth drafting)
rubrics_metrics.description: When constructing a proof, write the initial assumption and the desired conclusion first, then fill the intervening logical steps—possibly alternating between the two ends until they meet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sketching strategy helps focus the proof. After drafting, rewrite in clean paragraph form for presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use accepted standard facts without proof when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Some widely known results (division algorithm, unique factorization into primes, arithmetic properties) may be assumed as facts in subsequent proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State which standard facts are being used. If necessary for the course, reference where these facts are proved (the book refers to later sections). Do not assume obscure or unproven claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show equality by proving both inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: To show two quantities are equal, prove m ≤ n and n ≤ m (or m < n and n < m when strictness applies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This two-sided comparison is a standard method; the book uses lcm examples to illustrate proving m<n and n<m to conclude m=n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backward reasoning: work from desired conclusion to known facts, then reverse
rubrics_metrics.description: To find a proof path, it can help to work backward from the conclusion to something obviously true; then reverse those steps in the final proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to prove an inequality about square roots, square both sides and manipulate to an evidently true statement, then reverse the steps (being careful with sign/positivity issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish logical forms of theorems (conditional, biconditional, others)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most theorems are conditional ('If P then Q'), some are biconditional (P iff Q), and some state facts outright; be aware of their logical form when proving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A biconditional can be proved by proving two conditionals. Interpret definitions often written as 'if' to mean 'if and only if' by convention when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about variable domains and hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: State clearly the domain and conditions on variables (e.g., 'let a,b,c be integers', 'x and y positive numbers') before proceeding with a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many steps depend on these hypotheses (e.g., dividing by positive quantities). Omitting domain information can render steps invalid or ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use correct logical case partitioning (partition into disjoint cases when convenient)
rubrics_metrics.description: In counting or proof problems, partition the set of possibilities into disjoint cases and sum results when intersections are empty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: break 'strings with odd number of 1s' into cases with 1,3,5,7 ones; ensure the sets are pairwise disjoint so the addition principle applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition principle for disjoint sets
rubrics_metrics.description: If A1, A2, ..., An are sets with Ai ∩ Aj = ∅ whenever i ≠ j, then |⋃Ai| = |A1| + |A2| + ... + |An|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to reduce counting of a union of disjoint classes to counting each class separately. Confirm disjointness before applying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion–exclusion for two sets
rubrics_metrics.description: For finite sets A and B, |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This corrects double counting of elements in the intersection. Example: count hands that are all red or all face cards by subtracting red face-card hands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion–exclusion for three (and more) sets
rubrics_metrics.description: For three sets A,B,C: |A ∪ B ∪ C| = |A| + |B| + |C| − |A ∩ B| − |A ∩ C| − |B ∩ C| + |A ∩ B ∩ C|. The general pattern alternates inclusion and exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when sets overlap; recognize that if all pairwise intersections are empty the formula reduces to the addition principle. Use the general n-set inclusion–exclusion when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use combinatorial selection formulas (n choose k)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count subsets, strings, or hands by selecting k elements from n: use binomial coefficients C(n,k) (written (n choose k)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: number of 3-card red hands = C(26,3); number of binary strings with three 1s = C(7,3). Use combinatorial or algebraic reasoning to justify the choice formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pascal's triangle as computational and conceptual tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange binomial coefficients in Pascal's triangle: each entry (other than 1s at ends) equals the sum of the two entries above it, and Row n lists coefficients for (x+y)^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the recursive Pascal construction to compute coefficients without the closed formula; consult Row n to expand (x+y)^n and read coefficients directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binomial theorem: coefficients of (x+y)^n equal binomial coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: For non-negative integer n, (x+y)^n = Σ_{k=0}^n C(n,k) x^{n−k} y^k; Row n of Pascal's triangle lists these coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the binomial theorem to expand powers of binomials and to extract specific coefficients; the book accepts the theorem and uses it in counting exercises (proof deferred to exercises/chapter 10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct algebraic manipulation for inequality proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving inequalities involving roots or rational expressions, use algebraic operations valid under the hypotheses (e.g., factor, divide by positive quantities, square both sides when nonnegative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to prove sqrt(x) < sqrt(y) when x<y and both positive, manipulate (√x − √y)(√x + √y) < 0 and divide by √x+√y > 0. Always check sign/positivity before dividing or squaring.
